docs.title: About this project
docs.text:
Welcome to this comprehensive DevOps Engineering Knowledge Base!. This a structured learning resource created to help students, aspiring DevOps engineers, and IT professionals master modern DevOps practices through organized, high-quality documentation.

This project was built from detailed study notes taken while following a complete DevOps learning journey. Instead of scattered notes, every lesson has been carefully transformed into well-structured documentation that is easy to read, understand, and revisit. Each topic is presented in a logical sequence, allowing you to learn step by step or jump directly to a specific concept whenever you need a quick refresher.

The knowledge base currently contains 150+ lecture notes covering the core technologies and tools used by modern DevOps engineers, including Linux, Git, Bash Scripting, Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Argo CD, Terraform, Ansible, AWS, Azure, Python for DevOps, AI-Assisted DevOps, Observability, Monitoring, and many other essential concepts.

Every note is designed to be more than just a summary. Lessons include detailed explanations, practical examples, architecture diagrams, command references, configuration breakdowns, best practices, troubleshooting tips, and interview-focused insights. The goal is to create a reliable reference that supports both deep learning and fast revision without having to rewatch entire videos.

Whether you are starting your DevOps journey, preparing for technical interviews, revising concepts before certification exams, or searching for a specific command or configuration, this documentation is designed to save you time and strengthen your understanding.

This is an evolving knowledge base that will continue to grow with new topics, updated best practices, and emerging DevOps technologies, making it a valuable long-term reference for continuous learning and professional development.

docs.title: Scaffolding New Days
docs.text:
This project ships with a generator so you never hand-write folder structure or nav entries for 160 days.

python scripts/generate_course.py

What it does:

  1. Reads scripts/topics.yaml — a simple day, title, module list
  2. Creates docs/devops-course/day-XXX/index.md from the template (skips any file that already exists, so it's safe to re-run)
  3. Creates a .pages file per day setting its sidebar title to Day XXX – Topic Name
  4. Regenerates docs/devops-course/.pages so the sidebar is grouped by module, in the exact order defined in topics.yaml

To add Day 161+: add one row to scripts/topics.yaml, re-run the script. Nothing else changes — not mkdocs.yml, not any other file.

scripts/topics.yaml (excerpt)
- day: 161
  module: "Module 13: Advanced Kubernetes"
  title: "Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)"

docs.title: Fundamentals of DevOps (~25 days)
docs.text:
Don't skip the prerequisites

A common mistake: Jumping straight into Linux or Docker without first understanding What DevOps actually is and Where it fits in the software development life cycle (SDLC). Skipping this makes every tool you learn afterward harder to contextualize. You'll know how without knowing why.

docs.title: Learning order within this step:
docs.text:
1. What is DevOps & Why DevOps - The non-negotiable prerequisite.
  2. DevOps in the SDLC - How it accelerates software delivery.
  3. Linux fundamentals only - Not 2–3 months of Linux. Just enough to:
    • Understand why Linux is preferred over Windows for this work
    • Create and SSH into a Linux VM
    • Use the Top 50 shell commands DevOps engineers use day-to-day (a very common interview topic)
  4. Git & GitHub - Version control fundamentals that DevOps engineers use for infrastructure-as-code, not just app code. Pick GitHub specifically(free, has AI features, and the whole open-source ecosystem lives there - a talking point in interviews).
  5. Configuration management basics - Ansible fundamentals only.
  6. Terraform fundamentals only - Not 30–60 days of Terraform. Terraform depends on knowing a cloud platform's services first, so going deep here is wasted effort.
  7. Containerization - Docker - What containers are, how they differ from VMs, Docker architecture, networking, volumes/storage, image creation, plus a hands-on container project.
  8. Kubernetes fundamentals - Architecture, creating a cluster, Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, ConfigMaps, Secrets, CRDs, Helm, Kustomize, Ingress, and the Gateway API.
  9. CI/CD basics - Jenkins + GitHub Actions for CI, ArgoCD for CD (called out as the current in-demand combination for job descriptions).
  10. Advanced Linux - This is deliberately placed after the above, not before: folder structure, log management, process management, memory management, and day-to-day sysadmin tasks DevOps engineers actually do.

Must-have vs. good-to-have

Kubernetes especially can become a bottomless rabbit hole. You could study it for a year and still find more. For your first job, learn the must-have list above; save deep-dive Kubernetes mastery for after you're employed and being paid to learn it.

docs.title: Step 2 — Pick ONE Cloud Platform (~20–25 days)
docs.text:
If you choose AWSIf you choose Azure

Skip every Azure video in the course. Learning order:

  1. Cloud computing fundamentals (mostly platform-agnostic)
  2. IAM — users, roles, permissions (spend real time here — this is an ongoing administrative responsibility in the job, not a one-time setup task)
  3. Compute — EC2, Auto Scaling Groups, Load Balancers, launch templates
  4. Networking — VPC, security groups, Route 53
  5. Storage — S3
  6. Databases
  7. CI/CD services on AWS
  8. Containers — ECR (registry), ECS, EKS
  9. Serverless
  10. Compliance & security services, AWS Config
  11. Cloud migration strategies + a real-time AWS project

Skip every AWS video in the course. The same category order applies: fundamentals → IAM → compute → networking → storage → databases → CI/CD → containers → serverless → compliance/security → a real-time Azure project.

The #1 mistake in this step

Do not complete both AWS and Azure. Research which one is more in demand in your target location, commit to one, and master it. Splitting focus across two clouds is the instructor's most repeated warning in this roadmap.

docs.title: Step 3 — Infrastructure as Code: Terraform (~10 days)
docs.text:
You already covered Terraform fundamentals in Step 1. This step goes deeper, now that you understand cloud services well enough for the tool to make sense:

  • Providers
  • State management & state locking
  • Provisioners
  • Workspaces
  • Modules
  • Importing existing resources into Terraform
  • Vault integration for secrets
  • Drift detection

Why not Pulumi or Crossplane?

Both are gaining traction and the course covers them separately, but for your first DevOps role and first round of interviews, Terraform is still what most companies use and what most interviewers will ask about.

docs.title: Step 4 — Python for DevOps (~10 days, 16 videos)
docs.text: Not mastery — just enough Python to automate what shell scripting handles awkwardly. Suggested order: Python vs. shell (when to use which) → data types & keywords → functions/modules/packages → CLI arguments & operators → conditionals → lists/tuples/loops → file management → dictionaries → file operations → boto3 (AWS SDK for Python) → three real-time projects you can describe in interviews and add to your resume.

docs.title: Step 5 — AI-Assisted DevOps (~10 days, 10–15 videos)
docs.text:
New for 2026 — the instructor frames this as the differentiator that makes a resume stand out, not a strict must-have.

  • AI fundamentals & prompt engineering (zero-shot, multi-shot prompting)
  • Your first GenAI project for DevOps
  • Running models locally with Ollama
  • AI-assisted shell scripting
  • AIOps concepts and an AIOps project
  • Building your first AI agent with the CrewAI framework
  • Docker Model Runner (DMR)
  • An internal-documentation AI agent (CrewAI)
  • Enterprise AI platforms — setting up an agent in Retool

If you're a fresher

Even without production experience, being able to say "I know how to apply AI to DevOps workflows" is a meaningful interview differentiator.

docs.title: Step 6 — Observability (~5–6 days, ~10 videos)
docs.text:
Why this is no longer optional

In prior years, observability was a "good to have." Starting in the second half of 2025, most DevOps job descriptions began listing basic observability as a requirement — hence its promotion to a full step here.

Covers: Prometheus, Grafana, the ELK stack, Jaeger, OpenTelemetry, hands-on projects, and — recently added — PagerDuty (only ~20–30 minutes of content, but worth knowing how on-call paging works in practice).

docs.title: Study Cadence
docs.text:
The instructor's honest take

Courses + 2–3 hours on weekends only → "leads you nowhere." Whether or not you follow a paid course, 2–3 focused hours every day is the actual requirement behind the "3 months" estimate.

Commitment Realistic Total Timeline 2–3 hrs/day, daily ~3 months (as designed) 2–3 hrs, weekends only Not recommended — the instructor explicitly warns this doesn't work

docs.title: Why AI Hasn't Killed DevOps Hiring
docs.text: A note the instructor makes explicitly: development and testing roles have seen real reductions from AI/LLM tooling, but DevOps — being fundamentally an operations discipline — has been much less affected so far, since current large language models are still comparatively weak at operations work. This is offered as context, not a guarantee — worth treating as one person's read on the market rather than settled fact.

docs.title: DevOps Engineering Course
docs.text:
All lessons are categorized and organized in a logical learning sequence for easy navigation. GET START with Day 001 or explore any specific lesson based on your learning needs.

  • Day 001 - What is DevOps? Why DevOps? How to Introduce Yourself in a DevOps Interview

docs.title: Day 001 - What is DevOps? Why DevOps? How to Introduce Yourself in a DevOps Interview
What we cover in this lesson?
docs.text:
There are 04 classic DevOps-interview questions that every beginner must be able to answer confidently.

  1. What is DevOps?
  2. Why DevOps (why did it come into existence)?
  3. How do you introduce yourself for a DevOps role?
  4. What are your day-to-day activities as a DevOps engineer?

STUDY TIP

In real interviews, these four questions are often asked back-to-back at the very start of the conversation. If you stumble here, the interviewer may lose confidence in you within the first five minutes. So this material is disproportionately high-value for the time it takes to learn.

docs.title: Why This Matters?
docs.text:
• These four questions are not tool-specific. You don't need to know Jenkins, Kubernetes, or Terraform to answer them.
  • They test whether you understand the purpose and mindset of DevOps, not just the tooling.
  • Getting these wrong early in an interview can end the conversation before your technical skills are even discussed.
  • The Day 01 lesson is deliberately kept simple and jargon-light. Advanced concepts like Containerization, Kubernetes, and Cloud-Services are explicitly deferred to later episodes so beginners aren't overwhelmed.

docs.title: The Problem With "Textbook" Definitions
docs.text:
The instructor notes that there are hundreds of definitions of DevOps depending on the source: - AWS has its own definition. - Red Hat has a different one. - Every vendor tends to frame DevOps around its own tools.

Rather than memorizing one vendor's definition, we are going to build up a definition from first principles, layer by layer.

docs.title: Layer 01 - DevOps is a Culture, Not a Tool
docs.text:
Core idea

DevOps is a culture / practice an organization adopts to increase its ability to deliver applications.

  • The end goal of every organization — Amazon, Flipkart, or a small startup — is to deliver something to the customer.
  • Delivery speed is the single biggest business driver behind DevOps.

One-line definition (v1):

"DevOps is a culture that improves an organization's ability to deliver applications."

docs.title: Layer 2 - Why Delivery Speed Matters (Examples from the video)
docs.text:
Example 1 — Generic App (V1 → V2): If example.com takes 10 days to move a new version of its application from V1 to V2 through Dev → Staging → Production, that is considered slow and a poor practice.

Example 2 — PUBG bug/feature scenario: If there's a security issue or a new feature ready in PUBG, and it takes 10 days to ship it, that's a problem — because the fix should reach users almost immediately.

Example 3 — Android security patch: If a vulnerability is discovered on Android that could let a hacker access a phone, Android needs to: 1. Build a fix. 2. Push a new version. 3. Get users to auto-upgrade.

Ideally this entire cycle happens in hours, or at most 1–2 days — not weeks.

🎯 Takeaway: The faster and more reliably you can move code from a developer's machine to the customer, the more "DevOps mature" your organization is.

docs.title: Layer 3 - Is DevOps Only About Speed of Delivery?
docs.text:
A common misconception (explicitly called out in the video): people equate DevOps with CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) alone.

CI/CD = Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery — the practice of automatically building, testing, and deploying code changes frequently and reliably. (Term mentioned in video; expanded here for clarity.)

The instructor stresses: delivery speed is necessary but not sufficient. Speed without the following three things is dangerous.

docs.title: Layer 4 - The Manufacturing Analogy (Chips/Biscuits Factory)
docs.text:
To explain why speed alone isn't enough, the instructor steps away from software and uses a factory analogy:

Imagine a company manufacturing chips (potato chips / biscuits). If it automates its factory so a full batch is produced in one day instead of many days — is that good enough?

  • From the manufacturer's side → Automation ✅ (fast production)
  • From the customer's side → Speed alone doesn't matter if the product is bad. Customers care about Quality.
  • To make sure quality stays consistent, the factory needs Monitoring — someone/something has to flag it immediately if quality or the automated process breaks down.
  • And to catch problems before they reach the customer, the factory needs Testing.

This analogy maps directly onto software delivery.

docs.text:

      │ Remove     │   │ Ensure the  │      │ Observability)│  │ Continuous│

Pillar What it means Why it matters Automation Removing manual/human steps from build, deploy, and infra processes Speeds up delivery, removes human error Quality Application/code must meet a defined quality bar Fast delivery of a broken product is worthless Monitoring (a.k.a. Observability) Continuously watching the system so issues are reported automatically Lets teams react to failures before customers are badly affected Testing Continuous, ideally automated, testing throughout the pipeline Underpins both quality and safe automation

📝 Note from the instructor: Monitoring and Observability are described as "hand in hand" — closely related terms that will be explored together in a later, dedicated session.

docs.title: 2.7 Final Consolidated Definition (v2 — the one to memorize)
docs.text:
"DevOps is a process of improving application delivery by ensuring there is proper automation in place, by ensuring the application/code quality is maintained, by ensuring continuous monitoring, and by ensuring continuous testing."

The instructor explicitly says this is the ideal, complete definition for Day 1 — good enough to give confidently in an interview.

docs.title: 2.8 What NOT to Say (Scope Control for Day 1)
docs.text:
The instructor deliberately excludes these advanced terms from today's definition — not because they're wrong, but because they'll be covered properly in later episodes: - Cloud-native - Serverless - Shift-left

💡 Interview tip: It's fine to give a clean, simple, correct definition as a fresher. Over-stuffing your answer with buzzwords you can't explain is riskier than giving a solid basic answer.

docs.title: 2.9 Sample Interview Answer — "What is DevOps?"
docs.text: "DevOps is a process of improving the application delivery by ensuring there is proper automation, with application/code quality that is maintained, and by ensuring there is continuous monitoring and continuous testing in place."

docs.title: 2.10 The Business Outcome
docs.text: Example given: if example.com currently ships a release every 2 weeks, a DevOps engineer's job is to help bring that down toward 1 week (or less) — without sacrificing automation, quality, monitoring, or testing.

docs.title: 3.1 Setting the Scene
docs.text:
• Developer → writes the application code.
  • Customer → the person who ultimately uses the application (web app, Android app, static site, etc.)
  • The whole point of a company's existence is to get code from the developer safely and quickly into the customer's hands.

docs.title: 3.2 How It Worked ~10 Years Ago (Pre-DevOps Era)
docs.text:
Back then, there was no single "DevOps engineer" role. Instead, delivery required three separate, siloed roles, each doing one piece of manual work:

Role Responsibility System Administrator Provisions the server (and the application server) that will host the app. Before cloud platforms like AWS were common, this meant using VMware, OpenStack, or hypervisors like Xen on physical/bare-metal machines. Tester Tests the deployed application on the server the sysadmin created. Build & Release Engineer Takes the tested app and promotes it forward — first to a pre-production/staging environment, then (after re-testing) to production for the customer. (Developer, for context) Writes the code and checks it into a centralized version control system — e.g. SVN or CVS — so multiple developers can share code from one place.

ℹ️ Terms explained: - SVN (Apache Subversion) and CVS (Concurrent Versions System) — early centralized version control systems used before tools like Git became standard. Mentioned in the video as examples of where developers "checked in" code. - VMware / OpenStack — virtualization/cloud platforms used to provision servers before AWS-style public cloud became dominant. - Xen — a hypervisor used to create virtual servers on physical ("bare metal") hardware. - Bare metal — a physical, non-virtualized server. The video notes that "before 10 years, everything was bare metal." - Application server — the software layer on a server that actually hosts/runs the deployed application (distinct from the server/OS itself).

docs.title: 3.3 The Old Workflow, Visualized
docs.text:
[Developer]
     │  writes code, commits to
     ▼
 [Central Repo: SVN / CVS]
     │
     ▼
 [System Administrator]
     │  provisions Server + Application Server
     ▼
 [App deployed on Server]
     │
     ▼
 [Tester]
     │  tests the app on that server
     ▼
 [Build & Release Engineer]
     │  promotes app forward
     ▼
 [Pre-Prod / Staging Environment]
     │  re-tested
     ▼
 [Build & Release Engineer]
     │  promotes again
     ▼
 [Production Server]  ────────────────►  [Customer]

     Total elapsed time for one release: ~10 days
     (example figure used by the instructor — could be more or less
      depending on the org, but the process was consistently slow)

docs.title: 3.4 Why Was It So Slow?
docs.text:
The instructor pinpoints the root cause plainly:

Multiple separate teams + manual, human-driven handoffs = slow delivery.

  • Every handoff between Developer → Sysadmin → Tester → Build/Release Engineer → Production required coordination, waiting, and manual work.
  • There was no single owner responsible for the entire pipeline end-to-end.
  • This inefficiency — not any single tool being "missing" — is what caused the DevOps movement to emerge.

docs.title: 3.5 What Changed With DevOps
docs.text:
• Instead of three-plus siloed teams, DevOps consolidates delivery responsibility into one collaborative team/role.
  • Because there's no longer a rigid set of separate departments, DevOps has to be a culture — a shared way of working — rather than a fixed job description.
  • Part of that culture is being willing to adopt new tools quickly. Example given: if your CTO identifies a new tool that improves efficiency, a DevOps engineer needs the mindset to adapt and pivot — this adaptability is itself a defining trait of the culture.

docs.title: 3.6 Old vs. New — Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text: Aspect Before DevOps (~10 years ago) With DevOps Teams involved Sysadmin, Tester, Build & Release Engineer (separate) One collaborative team/engineer Process Manual handoffs at every stage Automated pipeline Infra Bare metal, VMware, OpenStack, Xen hypervisors Often cloud platforms (e.g. AWS) Release cycle Days to weeks (e.g. ~10 days) Hours to a couple of days Mindset Fixed role, fixed process Cultural adaptability, continuous improvement Core enablers N/A (manual) Automation, Quality, Monitoring, Testing

docs.title: 3.7 Sample Interview Answer — "Why DevOps?"
docs.text: "Before DevOps, delivering an application required multiple separate teams — a system administrator to provision servers, a tester to validate the app, and a build & release engineer to promote it through environments. Because every handoff was manual and teams worked in silos, releases were slow — sometimes taking 10 days or more. DevOps emerged to solve this by bringing these responsibilities into a single collaborative culture built around automation, quality, monitoring, and testing — which dramatically speeds up and improves the reliability of delivery."

docs.title: 4. How to Introduce Yourself in a DevOps Interview
4.1 Common Mistakes (What the Instructor Has Seen Go Wrong)
docs.text:
• Candidates rush their self-introduction into one or two minutes, believing that's a hard rule. It isn't. Take the time you genuinely need.
  • Candidates omit their prior background, which makes it harder for the interviewer to understand their fit.
  • Candidates exaggerate experience — e.g., claiming 10 years of DevOps experience — which is not credible, since DevOps as a widely-known practice has really only been popular for the last 7–8 years.

⚠️ Don't say: "My organization adopted DevOps 10 years ago" or "I have 10 years of DevOps experience." These claims don't hold up and can lose the interviewer's trust immediately.

docs.title: 4.2 The Recommended Structure
docs.text:
A good self-introduction has three parts, in this order:

Part 1 — Current DevOps experience State how many years you've worked specifically as a DevOps engineer (e.g., "4–5 years").

Part 2 — Prior background (very important) Mention what you did before DevOps. Common prior roles mentioned in the video: - System Administrator - Build & Release Engineer - Server Administrator - Java Developer / Python Developer - Automation Engineer

💡 Why this matters (interviewer's perspective, as explained in the video): If a candidate previously worked as a system administrator and the company uses AWS heavily, the interviewer can immediately see value: this person likely understands server administration and could help with automation or migrating on-prem infrastructure to the cloud. Your background gives the interviewer a mental model of where you'll add value.

Part 3 — Roles & responsibilities, mapped to the Four Pillars Describe your day-to-day contributions using the same four pillars from Section 2: - "I take care of automation..." - "I ensure quality is maintained for the applications..." - "I have set up continuous monitoring..." - "I have automated testing into the DevOps lifecycle..."

Optional Part 4 — Tools & Technologies The instructor says this is optional and not strongly recommended at the introduction stage, but if asked, you can mention things like:

Category Example Tool (as mentioned in video) CI/CD GitHub Actions Container Orchestration Kubernetes Configuration Management Ansible Infrastructure Automation (IaC) Terraform

The instructor deliberately keeps tool-talk minimal on Day 1 so beginners aren't overwhelmed — this will be expanded in later sessions.

docs.title: 4.3 What If You're a Fresher?
docs.text:
If you have no prior experience, keep it simple and honest:

"I just started working as/learning to be a DevOps engineer. I'm passionate about learning DevOps..." — then optionally speak to what you've been learning.

You are not expected to invent a fake background.

docs.title: 4.4 Self-Introduction Template
docs.text:
1. WHO YOU ARE NOW
   "I am a DevOps Engineer with [X] years of experience in DevOps."

2. WHERE YOU CAME FROM
   "Prior to that, I worked as a [System Administrator /
    Build & Release Engineer / Server Administrator /
    Java Developer / Python Developer / Automation Engineer]."
   (Freshers: "I recently started learning DevOps and I'm passionate
    about it.")

3. WHAT YOU DO DAY-TO-DAY (map to the 4 pillars)
   "In my current role, I take care of:
      - Automation      → [what you automate]
      - Quality         → [how you ensure app/code quality]
      - Monitoring       → [how you monitor systems]
      - Testing         → [how testing is integrated]"

4. (OPTIONAL, if asked) TOOLS
   "I work with tools like GitHub Actions for CI/CD, Kubernetes for
    container orchestration, Ansible for configuration management,
    and Terraform for infrastructure automation."

docs.title: 4.5 Interview Do's and Don'ts Cheat Sheet
docs.text: ✅ Do ❌ Don't Take the time you need — there's no strict 1–2 minute rule Rush your intro just because you think it must be short Mention your real prior background (even non-DevOps roles) Omit your background — it helps the interviewer place you Be honest about years of experience Inflate your years of DevOps experience Map your responsibilities to Automation / Quality / Monitoring / Testing Just list tool names with no context Let freshers say they're new and passionate Pretend to have experience you don't have

docs.title: 5. Consolidated Glossary (All Terms Mentioned in the Video)
docs.text: Term Definition (as used/implied in the video) DevOps A culture/practice that improves an organization's ability to deliver applications, built on automation, quality, monitoring, and testing. CI/CD Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery — commonly (and, per the instructor, too narrowly) equated with "DevOps" by beginners. Automation Removing manual steps from delivery processes. Quality Ensuring the application/code meets required standards. Monitoring / Observability Continuously watching systems so issues are automatically detected and reported. Testing Continuous validation of the application to catch defects, underpinning both quality and safe automation. System Administrator Pre-DevOps role responsible for provisioning servers and application servers. Tester Pre-DevOps role responsible for validating the deployed application. Build & Release Engineer Pre-DevOps role responsible for promoting the application through environments (e.g., staging → production). Server Administrator Another pre-DevOps role tied to managing server infrastructure. SVN / CVS Centralized version control systems used for shared code repositories before Git became dominant. VMware / OpenStack Pre-cloud virtualization/infrastructure platforms. Xen A hypervisor used to virtualize bare-metal servers. Bare metal Physical (non-virtualized) server hardware. Application server The layer on a server that actually hosts/runs a deployed application. Pre-Prod / Staging An intermediate environment where an app is re-tested before reaching production. Production The live environment serving real customers. Cloud-native (Named but explicitly deferred to a future episode — not explained in Day 1.) Serverless (Named but explicitly deferred to a future episode — not explained in Day 1.) Shift-left (Named but explicitly deferred to a future episode — not explained in Day 1.) GitHub Actions Example CI/CD tool mentioned. Kubernetes Example container orchestration tool mentioned. Ansible Example configuration management tool mentioned. Terraform Example infrastructure automation (IaC) tool mentioned.

docs.title: 6. Commands / Code Covered in This Session
docs.text: None. Day 1 of this course is entirely conceptual — it covers definitions, history, and interview framing. No CLI commands, config files, YAML, or scripts were demonstrated in this video. Tool names (GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Ansible, Terraform) were mentioned only as examples of technology categories, with no commands or syntax shown. Expect hands-on commands to begin in later episodes of the 40-day series.

docs.title: 7. Quick-Recap Cheat Sheet (For Fast Revision)
docs.text:
• DevOps in one line: A culture that improves an organization's ability to deliver applications, powered by Automation + Quality + Monitoring + Testing.
  • DevOps ≠ just CI/CD. CI/CD is part of it, but quality, monitoring, and testing are equally core.
  • Why DevOps exists: Before it, delivery needed 3 separate siloed roles (Sysadmin, Tester, Build & Release Engineer) with fully manual handoffs → releases took ~10 days. DevOps merges this into one collaborative culture to drastically cut that time.
  • Self-intro formula: Current DevOps experience → Prior background → Responsibilities mapped to the 4 pillars → (optional) tools.
  • Golden rule for interviews: Be honest about experience; your prior background (even non-DevOps) is valuable context for the interviewer, not something to hide.
  • Fourth interview question ("day-to-day activities") was named but not covered in Day 1 — flagged here so you know to look for it in a later session rather than assuming it was answered.
